issues.legal_issue: A land bought for a price at public auction is not treated as granted land merely because the document recording the transaction is titled as a certificate of grant.
material_facts: The landholder’s predecessor obtained the land through a public auction and paid a purchase price.
Although the document was titled as a certificate of grant, its recitals described a public-auction purchase for a price.
A revenue record also showed that the land was sold for a price, and the administrative authorities found that it had been purchased rather than granted.
The applicants sought cancellation of the subsequent transfer and restoration of the land under legislation concerning transfers of certain lands.
issues.conclusion: The land was purchased at public auction for a price and was not granted land within the relevant rules; accordingly, the statutory prohibition applicable to transfers of granted land did not apply.
issues.legal_principle: The prohibition in Section 4 of the Karnataka Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prohibition of Transfer of Certain Lands) Act, 1978 applies to granted land. Rule 43(8) of the Mysore Land Revenue Rules concerns land granted free or at an upset price. The nature of a document or transaction is determined by reading the document as a whole, considering its recitals and the evidence, rather than relying on its title alone. The Court relied on Vidhyadhar v. Manikrao, (1999) 3 SCC 573; Subbegowda (Dead) by LRs v. Thimmegowda (Dead) by LRs, (2004) 9 SCC 734; and Bishwanath Prasad Singh v. Rajendra Prasad, (2006) 4 SCC 432.

rule.if: land_transfer_restoration_proceeding and auction_purchase_for_price and (document_recitals_show_purchase or supporting_records_show_purchase)

predicates.land_transfer_restoration_proceeding: A person sought cancellation of a transfer or restoration of land under a scheme governing transfers of certain lands.
predicates.auction_purchase_for_price: The predecessor of the person claiming the land acquired it at a public auction by paying a purchase price.
predicates.document_recitals_show_purchase: The recitals in the transaction document describe the land as purchased for a price rather than granted.
predicates.supporting_records_show_purchase: Records apart from the transaction document show that the land was purchased for a price.
predicates.granted_land_transfer_prohibition_does_n: The prohibition governing transfers of granted land does not apply to the land.

issues.definition: When a restoration proceeding concerns land acquired by public-auction purchase for a price, and the document recitals or supporting records show a purchase, the granted-land transfer prohibition does not apply.

issues.legal_issue: Certiorari does not permit a reviewing court to reappraise evidence or correct a mere factual error in an administrative decision absent a qualifying jurisdictional or legal error causing grave injustice.
material_facts: The applicants sought certiorari to quash administrative orders determining that the land had been purchased at public auction rather than granted.
The authorities based their factual conclusion on the transaction document and revenue records.
The High Court declined to quash the orders, and the Supreme Court found no basis to disturb that decision.
issues.conclusion: The High Court correctly refused to quash the administrative orders because the factual finding was supported by the record and no qualifying error warranting certiorari was established.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 226 of the Constitution, certiorari is distinct from appellate review and is available for specified jurisdictional errors or where an authority acts illegally or improperly in exercising jurisdiction and causes grave miscarriage of justice. A factual finding may be corrected where it rests on legally inadmissible evidence, excludes admissible evidence, or has no evidentiary support. Mere factual error or reappreciation of evidence is insufficient; the error must be manifest and apparent and occasion grave injustice or gross failure of justice. The Court relied on Surya Dev Rai v. Ram Chander Rai, (2003) 6 SCC 675, and also addressed supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227.

predicates.certiorari_challenge_to_administrative_f: A party challenged an administrative authority’s decision through a proceeding seeking certiorari.
predicates.finding_supported_by_evidence: The administrative authority’s factual finding was supported by evidence in the record.
predicates.manifest_error_causing_grave_injustice: The finding involved a manifest legal or jurisdictional error that caused grave injustice or gross failure of justice.
predicates.certiorari_does_not_permit_fact_reapprai: The reviewing court may not reappraise the evidence merely to correct the factual finding.

issues.definition: When certiorari is sought against an administrative finding supported by evidence and no manifest error causing grave injustice is present, the reviewing court does not reappraise the facts.
